content: The studies reviewed here evaluate various interventions for pain management and labor outcomes, with a focus on their effects, quality of evidence, and clinical importance. Below are the findings presented in a clear and professional manner: 1. Acupuncture or Acupressure for Pain Management in Labor The evidence quality is very low due to significant design limitations in all contributing studies, high statistical heterogeneity (I² > 70%), wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect, and small sample sizes. Source: Smith CA, Collins CT, Crowther CA, Levett KM. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2011; (7): CD009232. 2. Hypnosis for Pain Management During Labor and Childbirth The intervention resulted in 163 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 126 fewer to 186 fewer) with low-quality evidence. Design limitations were present in all studies, with over 40% of the weight coming from studies with serious design flaws. Source: Madden K, Middleton P, Cyna AM, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012; (11): CD009356. 3. Aromatherapy for Pain Management in Labor The intervention showed 45 more events per 1,000 (range: 32 fewer to 144 more) with low-quality evidence. The evidence was limited by a single study with design flaws and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. Source: Smith CA, Collins CT, Crowther CA. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2011; (7): CD009215. 4. Biofeedback for Pain Management During Labor The intervention resulted in 83 more events per 1,000 (range: 140 fewer to 472 more) with very low-quality evidence. The evidence was based on a single study with serious design limitations, wide confidence intervals, few events, and a small sample size. Source: Barragán Loayza IM, Solà I, Juandó Prats C. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2011; (6): CD006168. 5. Intravenous Fluids for Shortening Labor Duration (Maternal Outcomes) The intervention showed 80 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 150 fewer to 24 more) with low-quality evidence. Limitations included small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and no events in some studies. Source: Dawood F, Dowswell T, Quenby S. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (6): CD007715. 6. Intravenous Fluids for Shortening Labor Duration (Infant Outcomes) The intervention resulted in 10 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 19 fewer to 93 more) with very low-quality evidence. Evidence was limited by design flaws, no events, and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. Source: Dawood F, Dowswell T, Quenby S. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (6): CD007715. 7. Oral Fluid and Food Intake During Labor (Maternal Outcomes) Restricting oral intake resulted in 5 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 33 fewer to 27 more) with moderate-quality evidence. However, other outcomes showed very low-quality evidence due to design limitations, statistical heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals. Source: Singata M, Tranmer J, Gyte GML. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (8): CD003930. 8. Oral Fluid and Food Intake During Labor (Infant Outcomes) The intervention showed 2 more events per 1,000 (range: 14 fewer to 23 more) with low-quality evidence. Limitations included design flaws, wide confidence intervals, and small sample sizes. Source: Singata M, Tranmer J, Gyte GML. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (8): CD003930. 9. Maternal Position and Mobility During the First Stage of Labor (Maternal Outcomes) The intervention resulted in 23 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 5 fewer to 36 fewer) with low-quality evidence. Evidence was limited by design flaws, statistical heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals. Source: Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (8): CD003934. 10. Maternal Position and Mobility During the First Stage of Labor (Infant Outcomes) The intervention showed 2 fewer events per 1,000 (range: 6 fewer to 15 more) with very low-quality evidence. Limitations included serious design flaws, wide confidence intervals, and small sample sizes. Source: Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013; (8): CD003934. Each intervention's evidence quality and clinical importance were assessed using the GRADE framework, highlighting the need for more robust and well-designed studies to draw definitive conclusions.
